title: Why Cangas tastes the way it does

lede.text: Vines grow on steep slate slopes in the southwest of Asturias. Winters are cold, summers are very hot, and Albarín Blanco is the preferred white grape.

terms.term: Vino de Calidad con Indicación Geográfica
terms.text: This traditional term may replace "Denominación de Origen Protegida" on the label.

terms.term: Crianza, Reserva, Gran Reserva, Añejo, Noble
terms.text: These five traditional terms may be used on Cangas wines.
These two terms may be used if the wine meets the conditions of the Spanish labelling decree (Real Decreto 1363/2011, Annex III).
The vintage year must appear on every protected wine, even if it was not aged.

chapters.title: Steep valleys in the southwest
paras: The Cangas vineyards lie in the southwest of Asturias. The land is very rugged. Most slopes are steep to very steep, and some are sheer.
The only flat ground is alluvial land on the valley floors. The Narcea and the Navia are the main rivers.
The zone covers seven municipalities and nine parishes of Tineo.

fly.label: The Cangas zone
fly.caption: The zone covers seven municipalities and nine parishes of Tineo, in the southwest of Asturias.

chapters.title: Cold winters, hot summers
paras: The Cantabrian range acts as a barrier. Clouds pile up on its northern slopes. A foehn effect brings dry, hot winds.
Mountains and deep, narrow valleys also bring a continental influence. The pliego calls the result a microclimate unique in Asturias.
Winter lows fall to about 10 °C below zero. Summer highs pass 30 °C, and a few days come close to 40 °C.
Rain is about 1,000 mm a year. That is 30% less than the rest of Asturias. Skies are clear more often, and some municipalities reach 2,000 hours of sun.
Growers choose slopes with good aspect, to catch as many hours of sun as they can.

fly.label: Cangas del Narcea
fly.caption: Some municipalities in the zone reach 2,000 hours of sun, clearly more than the rest of Asturias.

chapters.title: Slate and schist
paras: The rocks are Paleozoic and Precambrian, among the oldest in the Iberian Peninsula. Precambrian slate stands out.
The soils form on slate and schist. Sandstone adds a small share of sand.
They are not deeply developed, and they are stony. Their pH is about 6, which is acid but close to neutral.
The humus layer is 20 to 25 cm thick and rich in organic matter. The mineral layers reach 60 to 80 cm.
The texture is medium and water drains well. That stops waterlogging and erosion on the steep slopes.
The pliego says slate gives the wines their own character.

chapters.title: Albarín and Mencía
paras: Cangas wines may be made only from the grapes the pliego lists.
The preferred reds are Albarín Tinto and Carrasquín. Verdejo Negro and Mencía are preferred too.
Albarín Blanco is the preferred white.
Yields are capped at 8,000 kg per hectare for red grapes and 10,000 kg for white. Wine yield is capped at 56 hl per hectare for red and 70 hl for white.
Vines are planted at 3,000 to 6,000 per hectare. They are trained as bush vines or on wires, depending on the soil and the vineyard.
